lead: In the season of the Resurrection the Church thinks of those who have just been baptized and of all of us who were raised with Christ in baptism. Paul tells the Galatians that Christ has released them from slavery, and that what counts is “faith working through love”. In the Gospel Jesus opens the ears and loosens the tongue of a man who could not hear or speak well. Freedom in Paul and opening in Mark are one gift: the risen Lord releases what was bound so that we can hear his word and speak his praise. The words to watch are freedom, yoke and Ephphatha.

r.h: For freedom Christ has set us free
set: Paul had brought the Gospel to the Galatians, Gentiles in central Asia Minor. After he left, other teachers came and told them that to belong fully to God’s people they must also be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. For Paul this was not a small matter of custom. If a Gentile is told that circumcision is needed in order to be justified, then Christ alone is no longer enough. Chapters 3–4 have argued this from Abraham and from the two sons of Abraham; today’s verses draw the conclusion.

Paul is not attacking the Jewish people or Jewish practice. He was a Jew himself, and he speaks here to Gentile believers about what is required of them. His point is that righteousness comes by God’s grace in Christ, received in faith, and not by taking on the Law as a condition.
str: v. 1: the thesis: “For freedom Christ has set us free”; stand firm.
vv. 2–4: a solemn warning: to seek justification by the Law is to be cut off from Christ.
v. 5: the Christian way of waiting: by the Spirit, through faith, in hope.
v. 6: what really counts: faith working through love.
kw: Not the right to do anything at all, but release from slavery into sonship. A few verses later Paul adds: “do not use your freedom as an opportunity for self-indulgence, but through love become slaves to one another” (5:13).

The wooden beam on the neck of an ox. Jewish teachers could speak warmly of the “yoke of the Law” as a joyful service. Paul uses the image for anything that would put a believer back under slavery, and Jesus offers his own yoke as easy (Matthew 11:29–30).
The word from which “energy” comes. Faith is not idle. It is alive and at work, and its working is love.
vv: For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
The freedom is already given. Paul does not tell them to win it, but to “stand firm” in what they have received.
You who want to be justified by the law have cut yourselves off from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.
Strong words. To make anything else the ground of our justification is to step away from grace, which is the only ground.
the only thing that counts is faith working through love.
This is one of the clearest lines in Paul on faith and love together. Faith that saves is not a bare opinion; it is faith that loves. By grace, love is the very life of faith.
ch: The Council of Trent took up this verse when it taught that in justification faith is joined with hope and charity, since faith without them does not unite a person perfectly with Christ (Decree on Justification, chapter 7, in substance). Catholics and Lutherans, in their Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), were able to say together that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ, and not because of any merit of ours, and that this grace renews the heart and moves us to good works. Our good works are themselves the fruit of grace.

set: Jesus has been in the region of Tyre, where he healed the daughter of a Gentile woman (7:24–30). Now he takes a long road: north to Sidon and then down to the east side of the Sea of Galilee, into the Decapolis, the “ten cities”, a largely Gentile region. Earlier, the people of this same region had begged him to leave (5:17). Now they bring a man to him.
Mark keeps the Aramaic word that Jesus spoke, Ephphatha. It is one of the few places where the Gospels let us hear the Lord’s own language, the sister tongue of our Syriac.
str: vv. 31–32: the journey; a deaf man with a speech impediment is brought.
vv. 33–34: Jesus takes him aside, touches ears and tongue, looks up, sighs, and speaks.
vv. 36–37: the command to silence, and the crowd’s astonished praise.
kw: with an impediment in his speech

A very rare Greek word. In the Greek Old Testament it appears only in Isaiah 35:6, “the tongue of the speechless sing for joy”, in a promise of the day when God comes to save. Mark is hinting that this day has come.
Aramaic, which Mark translates for his readers. The command is spoken to the man, not only to his ears: the whole person is opened.
A deep groan. Jesus does not heal from a distance or without feeling. Paul uses the same family of words for creation and the Spirit groaning for redemption (Romans 8:22–26).
vv: He took him aside in private, away from the crowd, and put his fingers into his ears, and he spat and touched his tongue.
The healing begins with a meeting apart. The man cannot hear words, so Jesus speaks to him by touch, in a language he can understand.
Then looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.”
He looks to the Father before he speaks. The healing comes from the communion between the Son and the Father.
He has done everything well; he even makes the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.
Many readers hear an echo of creation, when God saw that everything he had made was very good (Genesis 1:31), and of Isaiah 35:5–6. In Jesus, God is making things new.
ch: Very early this healing was joined to baptism. St Ambrose explained to the newly baptized in Milan the rite called “Ephphatha”, in which the bishop touched their ears and nostrils before baptism, so that they might be opened to the word and to the fragrance of Christ (On the Mysteries, in substance). The Church sees in this man every believer whom Christ opens to hear the Gospel and to confess the faith. Those who have received the Word must also speak it: the crowd in the Decapolis could not keep silent.

qa: Why does Jesus tell them to tell no one, and why do they disobey?

Mark often shows Jesus asking for silence about his miracles. He did not want to be taken for a mere wonder-worker; who he is would be fully seen only on the Cross and in the Resurrection. The people cannot hold back their joy. Now that he is risen, the command is the opposite: go and proclaim it (Mark 16:15).
study: Paul says, “Stand firm” in the freedom Christ has given. What old yoke do I keep picking up again?
Jesus took the man aside before he healed him. Where could I go apart with the Lord this week, so that he can open my ears and loosen my tongue?
